solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Silly clowning around outside back of hut

indicators.note: going around or sitting outside something means wrapping it, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: clowning about is fooling

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter, so only the end is kept

parts.note: last letter of hut

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a bit of daft clowning going on around the back of a hut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' looks like part of the phrase 'clowning around', but here it joins 'outside' as the instruction to wrap FOOLING round T.
explanation.definitionFit: Footling is a British adjective meaning trivial, petty or silly, describing something not worth taking seriously.

clue.text: Vendetta not many'd spoken of

indicators.note: something spoken of is said out loud, so we want a word matching its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: not many is few, and the setter adds the contraction 'd to make it few'd

explanation.surface: An awkward line about a vendetta that few people would talk about.
explanation.walkthrough: The ugly contraction 'many'd' is the setter's signal: 'not many'd' is 'few'd', which is said exactly like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A vendetta is a prolonged bitter quarrel, often between families, which is what a feud is.

clue.text: Very rarely performing a nice varied 1930s song

indicators.note: something varied has been changed about, so these letters come in a new order

parts.note: a performer who is on is on stage
letters to be rearranged
Blue Moon is a Rodgers and Hart song from 1934

explanation.surface: A performer seldom sings a nicely varied old 1930s standard.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters sit between ON and the song title to spell ONCE IN A BLUE MOON.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something that happens only on the rarest occasions, exactly as seldom as a second full moon in a month.

clue.text: What a convict won't do for a budgie!

parts.note: surface reading: something a prisoner refuses to do
setter's reading: 'bird' is slang for a prison sentence, and no convict will enjoy doing time

explanation.surface: A joke about a prisoner's attitude to a pet budgerigar.
explanation.walkthrough: Doing bird is British slang for serving a jail term, so a convict won't love bird; read as one word, that is a small parrot.
explanation.definitionFit: Lovebirds are small affectionate parrots, and budgerigars are loosely called lovebirds as a similar small pet parrot.

clue.text: City don leaving capital to provide material …

parts.note: NY is New York

indicators.note: when something is leaving, it departs and is taken out of the word it was in

parts.note: the British capital city
taken as written, the letters to remove

explanation.surface: A university lecturer quits the capital to supply cloth to another city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' reads as an Oxbridge lecturer, but here it is just three letters to strike out of the capital's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Nylon is a synthetic fabric used for stockings and clothing, so it counts as a material.

clue.text: Keep new judge in the same cricket side

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within the others

parts.note: DO is short for ditto, meaning the same
N is the abbreviation for new
J is the abbreviation for judge
the on side is the leg side of a cricket field

explanation.surface: A selector asks to retain a fresh umpire with the same cricket team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep' looks like a verb, but it is the noun for a castle's strongest tower. The on side is the leg side of a cricket field.
explanation.definitionFit: A donjon is the old spelling of dungeon, meaning the central fortified tower of a castle, also called its keep.

clue.text: … partly for a chemical plant

indicators.note: partly means only a portion is used, so the letters sit inside a longer run of text

parts.note: letters running across the words

explanation.surface: Continuing 4 down: material is supplied, in part, for a chemical works.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links back to 4 down, but this clue stands alone: the letters run through 'for a chemical', and 'chemical plant' is a false phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Orache is a leafy herb of the goosefoot family, sometimes grown as a spinach substitute, so it is a plant.

clue.text: Versatile worker's flag initially overturned by autumn winds

parts.note: a jack is a small flag flown on a ship

indicators.note: initially points to the start of a word, so its first letter is kept

parts.note: first letter of overturned
fall is the American word for autumn
the trades are the trade winds

explanation.surface: A handyman's flag gets knocked over by autumn gales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overturned' looks like a reversal signal, but only its first letter is used. The 's stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names someone able to turn a hand to many different jobs, which is a versatile worker.

clue.text: Scholar, one barely recognisable outside Alabama

indicators.note: to be outside something is to surround it, so one piece wraps around another

parts.note: someone barely recognisable is wearing next to nothing, like a nudist
AL is the postal abbreviation for Alabama

explanation.surface: An academic has gone so native in Alabama he is barely recognisable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barely' pretends to mean scarcely; it really means naked, so the barely recognisable one is a nudist.
explanation.definitionFit: A naturalist is an expert who studies natural history, plants and animals, so the word fits a scholar.

clue.text: Unknown in C stream, one child's first alphabet

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: taken as written
algebra's unknowns are x, y and z
a rill is a small stream
Roman numeral one

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: first letter of child

explanation.surface: A child's first alphabet includes some mysterious letter by a stream.
explanation.walkthrough: The bare 'C' looks like a note or a grade, but it is simply the letter; Y goes after it and before RILL.
explanation.definitionFit: Cyrillic is the script used for Russian, Bulgarian and Serbian, so it names a particular alphabet.

clue.text: Rudely cursed at first by a French climber nursing injury

indicators.note: to nurse something is to hold it close, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: un is French for a

indicators.note: at first points to the start of a word, so only its opening letter is kept

parts.note: first letter of cursed
ivy is a climbing plant
ill as a noun means harm or injury

explanation.surface: A hurt French mountaineer swears rudely at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climber' suggests a mountaineer, but it is the plant IVY, which opens to take ILL.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting uncivilly means behaving without courtesy or good manners, which is the same as acting rudely.

clue.text: Former tax on a type of neckwear

parts.note: taken as written
scot was an old tax, surviving in scot-free

explanation.surface: A historical levy was charged on a kind of tie.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue, X 'on' Y puts X after Y, so the old tax follows A.
explanation.definitionFit: An ascot is a broad cravat-style tie worn looped at the throat, named after the racecourse, so it is neckwear.

clue.text: Doctor attending Light Infantry member

parts.note: LI is the military abbreviation for Light Infantry
MB is Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's degree

explanation.surface: A medic treats a soldier of the Light Infantry regiment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attending' suggests a doctor tending a patient, but it only means next to. MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a British medical degree.
explanation.definitionFit: Member has an older sense of a body part, especially an arm or leg, which is what a limb is.

clue.text: Our Bing? He could be the bloke next door!

indicators.note: could be suggests what the letters might become if arranged differently

parts.note: letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether the famous crooner Bing Crosby might be living next door.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital B makes Bing look like Crosby, but it is just four letters of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A neighbour is a person living in the adjacent house, the man or woman who lives beside you.

clue.text: Fuddy-duddies worry, seeing canvas on yard

parts.note: squares are old-fashioned, conventional people
to ail is to trouble or worry

explanation.surface: Old fogeys fret when they see a tent pitched in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yard' reads as a garden, but it is a ship's spar, and 'canvas' is sailcloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A square sail is a four-sided sail hung from a horizontal spar across the mast, so it is canvas on a yard.

clue.text: Figure in role of duke having noisy argument on phone?

parts.note: qua is Latin for in the capacity of
D is the abbreviation for duke

indicators.note: on the phone we hear sounds without seeing spelling, so the word is judged by how it is said

parts.note: a wrangle is a loud dispute; the silent w drops out in the spelling

explanation.surface: An actor playing a duke has a shouting match over the telephone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figure' suggests a person or number, but here it is a geometric shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A quadrangle is a plane shape with four angles and four sides, so it is a geometric figure.

clue.text: Bird which nests in northern university church

indicators.note: to nest in a place is to settle snugly inside it, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for northern
U is the abbreviation for university
which and that are interchangeable relative pronouns
CH is the abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: A bird that makes its home in a church at a northern university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Which' looks like a mere relative pronoun joining bird to its habits, but it supplies letters of its own and is the piece that nests.
explanation.definitionFit: The nuthatch is a small European songbird that climbs tree trunks head first, so it is a kind of bird.

clue.text: Highland Scot's verbal report of force eight wind, perhaps

indicators.note: a verbal report is spoken, so the word wanted matches the sound, not the spelling

parts.note: force eight on the Beaufort scale is a gale; 'perhaps' marks it as one example

explanation.surface: A Highlander gives a spoken account of a severe storm.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is'. Force eight is gale on the Beaufort wind scale.
explanation.definitionFit: A Gael is a Gaelic-speaking Celt, and in Scotland the term traditionally means a Highlander.

clue.text: Escape of liquid ultimately damages sacking

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the last letter of a word is kept

parts.note: last letter of damages
sacking a town is plundering it, which is pillage

explanation.surface: A leak in the end ruins some hessian sacks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sacking' suggests coarse cloth or dismissal, but here it means looting a town.
explanation.definitionFit: A spillage is an amount of fluid that has spilt or leaked out of its container, so an escape of liquid.

clue.text: Completely unknown person giving us support

parts.note: all as in 'all alone', meaning completely
algebra's unknowns are x, y and z

explanation.surface: A total stranger comes forward to back our cause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Completely unknown person' reads as one phrase, but the definition starts only at 'person'.
explanation.definitionFit: An ally is someone who sides with and helps another party, a friend or partner who backs you.

clue.text: Stores investing pounds in standard baked foods

parts.note: stock as an adjective means standard or usual

indicators.note: to invest is to clothe or surround, so one piece is placed within another

parts.note: pies are baked dishes
L is the abbreviation for pounds sterling, from libra

explanation.surface: Shops put money into ordinary bakery goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Investing pounds' sounds financial, but investing means enclosing: L goes inside PIES.
explanation.definitionFit: A stockpile is a reserve supply accumulated for future use, so stockpiles are stores.

clue.text: Proper woman retiring as governess

parts.note: due means proper or fitting, as in due care

indicators.note: retiring means going back, so this piece is read backwards

parts.note: a common woman's name

explanation.surface: A respectable lady withdraws from society to become a governess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retiring' reads as shy or leaving work, but it turns the name round.
explanation.definitionFit: A duenna is an older woman employed to act as chaperone and governess to young girls in Spanish and Portuguese families.

clue.text: Performer from Utah welcomed by one-time City worker

indicators.note: someone welcomed is taken in, so this piece is placed inside others

parts.note: ex means former
EC is the postcode of the City of London
UT is the postal abbreviation for Utah
the worker ant is the crossword's standard worker

explanation.surface: An American entertainer is greeted by a former banker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'City worker' looks like a banker, but the City (London's financial district) and the worker are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An executant is someone who carries out or performs something, especially a musician playing a piece.

clue.text: Old Italian poet's sons immersed in Chinese way of life

indicators.note: to be immersed in something is to be sunk inside it, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: the Tao is the Way in Chinese philosophy
S for son, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: An Italian poet's sons are steeped in Eastern philosophy.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's reads as possessive but stands for 'is'. Torquato Tasso wrote Jerusalem Delivered in the 16th century.
explanation.definitionFit: Tasso is a sixteenth-century Italian epic writer, best known for Jerusalem Delivered, so he is an old Italian poet.

clue.text: See about specialised knowledge

parts.note: lo is an old word for look or see
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: An instruction to look into expert knowledge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a container or reversal signal, but it simply gives RE.
explanation.definitionFit: Lore is a body of traditional or expert learning about a particular subject, such as folklore or bird lore.

clue.text: Alcoholic drink boozer finally concealed in coat

indicators.note: something concealed in another is hidden inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: a mac is a raincoat, short for mackintosh

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the last letter is kept

parts.note: last letter of boozer

explanation.surface: A drinker ends up hiding a bottle of spirits in his coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boozer' is British slang for a pub or a heavy drinker, but only its last letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Marc is a brandy distilled from the skins and pips left after grapes are pressed for wine, so it is an alcoholic drink.

clue.text: A scam involving introduction of ripe fruit

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: to involve is to include or take in, so one piece is placed within another

parts.note: a con is a swindle

indicators.note: an introduction is the opening, so only the first letter is kept

parts.note: first letter of ripe

explanation.surface: A fraud that involves passing off ripe fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fruit' suggests something juicy, but botanically a nut counts: the acorn is the oak's fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: The acorn is the nut produced by an oak tree, and in botany a nut is a kind of fruit bearing the seed.

clue.text: Accountant's woman, one fated to be disbelieved

parts.note: CA is a chartered accountant, with the 's kept
a woman's name

explanation.surface: An accountant's wife is doomed never to be believed.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s looks possessive but supplies a letter: CA's gives CAS before the name.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Trojan princess was cursed by Apollo to prophesy truly but never be believed.

clue.text: Liberal leader with a posh four-wheeled carriage

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: first letter of Liberal
and means with or plus
taken as written
U means upper-class, as in U and non-U

explanation.surface: A party leader rides in a grand horse-drawn coach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Posh' giving U comes from 1950s British talk of U (upper-class) and non-U speech and manners.
explanation.definitionFit: A landau is a horse-drawn four-wheeled vehicle with a folding hood, so it matches the description of a carriage.

clue.text: Variety of conifers connected with court

indicators.note: a variety is a different form of something, so these letters appear in a new order

parts.note: letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A particular type of pine tree is linked to a royal court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' suggests a palace setting among the trees, but it is a court of law.
explanation.definitionFit: Forensic describes evidence or methods used in legal proceedings, so it relates to law courts.
